opening.headline: The reason why AI reads receipt photos but does not know yesterday's news is explained through two axes: input format and knowledge cutoff.
body: When you upload a photo of your receipt to AI, it reads the items and amounts and organizes them. However, when you ask, “Tell me about the news that was announced yesterday,” they either say they don’t know or provide outdated information. You may be wondering why one works and the other doesn't, even though it's the same tool.

In this class, we will look at multimodal input, where the model receives various inputs such as images, files, and voices in addition to text, and the knowledge cutoff, which is only known up to the point at which the model learned. We then establish criteria to determine whether a question requires up-to-date information and determine when a web search connection is necessary.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of multimodal input and knowledge cutoff
You can distinguish between questions that require up-to-date information and questions that do not.

screens.title: It reads images, but doesn't know yesterday's news.
screens.lead: Read the two scenes side by side. The same AI can do one thing and not the other.

visual.alt: Two cards with a picture of a receipt on the left and a picture asking about yesterday's news on the right.
labels: Read and organize items and amounts
Please tell me what was announced yesterday
Information that is unknown or out of date

paragraphs: In Scene 1, the user uploads a photo of a receipt. AI reads the items and amounts in the photo and organizes them into a table. I just uploaded a photo without any additional tools and it worked accurately.

In Scene 2, the user asks, “Tell me what was announced yesterday.” This time, the AI ​​either says it doesn't know, or answers old information as if it were up-to-date. Why do the same tools react so differently?

This class is divided as follows. Scene 1 is a matter of input format, i.e. what type of input can be received. Scene 2 is a matter of what the model knows, i.e. the knowledge point. The two questions are on different axes and should be considered separately.

callout.label: Questions for this class
callout.text: What inputs can it receive, and does the model know until when?

screens.outro: First, let's recall your experience sending multiple types of input to an AI.

screens.title: Think about your experience sending files, images, and voices.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. There are no fields to enter or submit, so think about it first and then click it.

visual.alt: Illustration of three icons in a row representing a document, an image, and a voice.

items.prompt: If you have ever sent a file, image, or voice to AI, what was the result?
items.answer: Most of the time, “I read better than I think” and “I read strangely sometimes” come to mind together. The point of this class is that being able to read is different from reading accurately.

items.prompt: What input was read well and what was not read well?
items.answer: Clear photos and organized documents are easy to read, but blurry text, complicated tables, and noisy voices are often missed. Since each input format has its limitations, we will organize them by format in the following screen.

items.prompt: Have you ever asked for the latest news and the answer was different?
items.answer: If you've had that experience, you've encountered a problem with the point of knowledge, not the input format. This is a phenomenon that occurs because the model only knows the information up to the point of learning, and is the second axis of this class.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's first take a closer look at multimodal input.

screens.title: Multimodal input: Accepts more than just text
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how the three companies' documents describe image input.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: The Gemini documentation explains that the model was built from the ground up to be multimodal. Therefore, you can perform tasks such as image description, classification, and question-and-answer about images without learning a separate dedicated model. There are three ways to convey images: Public images are sent as URLs, small images are sent as base64-encoded inline data, and images to be reused in large files or multiple requests are uploaded to the File API.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: The OpenAI document says that recent language models can process and analyze image input, calling this ability vision. We provide guidance on whether you want to analyze an image or create a new image. The Responses API or Chat Completions API is used for analysis, and a separate image model is used for creation. The ChatGPT app allows you to request that images, diagrams, screenshots, and charts you upload be analyzed.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude's documentation provides three ways to send images. You can upload it like uploading a file in claude.ai, drag and drop it into the chat window, add it directly to a message in the console's Playground, or send it as an API request. In the API, images can be passed as base64 data, URL, or file_id returned by the Files API, and multiple images can be compared together in one request.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body: All three companies accept images as input along with text. And images are also calculated as tokens, units that the model divides and processes input into. The Gemini documentation explains that all inputs and outputs are processed as tokens, including image files. So there are limits and costs to the size and number of images.

screens.outro: If there are different input formats, what you can do and what you need to pay attention to are different for each format. Let’s look at it next.

screens.title: Things you can do and things to keep in mind for each input format
screens.lead: The following flashcards explain the uses and limitations of each input format. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

visual.alt: Four card front icons representing text, image, file, and voice respectively.

cards.back: This is the most basic input. Includes all questions, instructions, and pasted text. The model processes text by dividing it into units called tokens, so there is a limit to the length that can be viewed at one time, known as the context window.

You can upload photos, diagrams, screenshots, and charts to ask questions or ask for interpretation. The ChatGPT overview document explains that you can get help extracting content from images or interpreting what you see. However, being able to read and reading accurately are two different things, so blurry text and folded parts should be checked against the original.

Upload documents, spreadsheets, and presentations to summarize, extract information, or ask questions about the content. Depending on the format, there are restrictions on size, number, and type, and the available tools and models vary depending on the plan and settings.

If you upload a supported voice file, you can ask for the content or request dictation. The OpenAI documentation notes that speech understanding and dictation performance may vary depending on the language. It is safe to check important information against the recording.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the second axis, the point at which the model knows, the knowledge cutoff.

screens.title: Link knowledge cutoffs to web searches
screens.lead: Move the slider along the time axis. The time you ask a question changes how much the model knows and whether it needs to make discovery connections.

visual.alt: The horizontal time axis connecting the learning point and now and the search connection box on the right.

data.controlLabel: The point at which the question refers

stops.body: This is when the data is in the data the model was trained on. The model can answer based on this range and no search is required. However, not all of the content within the standard date is accurate, and as seen above, there may be errors or made-up content mixed in.

This happened right after the study was over. The model failed to learn this task. OpenAI help explains that the model is trained on data up to a certain point in time, and that events after that are not reflected in the response unless you use the tool. Rather than saying it doesn't know, the model may respond with similar old information.

This is a case where you are asking for information at this time. Typical examples are values ​​that change over time, such as exchange rates, weather, and today's news. These questions cannot be answered by the model alone; a connection such as a web search is needed to find the current value and display it with the source.

The model overview document indicates the knowledge cutoff for each model. In the Claude model overview table, these points are written in monthly units, and more detailed base dates are provided on a separate information page. This date marks the end of what the model knows. When choosing a model, this date is something to check along with performance.

According to the ChatGPT overview document, the search tool is used to find recent or real-time information and provide answers with sources. However, the range of tools available varies depending on your plan and settings, and is only used when search is turned on. You can tell if a search was used by checking if the web source appears in the input field or response.

screens.outro: Now that we've distinguished the two axes, let's apply them to two real-life examples.

screens.title: Commentary: Receipt image analysis
screens.lead: The instructor explains the question asking for the total of receipt photos step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Determine the nature of the question
steps.body: The question is, “What is the total of these receipts?” Where is the answer to this question? It's in the photo uploaded by the user. The first criterion is that the answer is entered as input along with the question.

steps.title: Determine what features you need
steps.body: The model can take an image as input and read it. Therefore, receipt analysis does not require up-to-date information and does not require web searches. Whether the receipt is from a few days ago or a long time ago has no bearing on the model's base date of knowledge.

steps.title: Check read limit
steps.body: However, there is a difference between being able to read a model and reading it accurately. Blurred text, folds, or crumpled numbers on receipts can be misread. For important values, such as sums, the results are checked against the original once received.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: This question is solved with multimodal input and no web search required. What you care about in this case is not the knowledge cutoff, but whether the picture is clear and whether the readings are correct. When choosing a function, the habit of first asking "Is the answer to this question in the input?" makes the decision easier.

screens.outro: This time, let's look at today's exchange rate inquiry, which the same AI cannot solve.

screens.title: Commentary: Why is today's exchange rate inquiry different?
screens.lead: The table below compares receipt analysis and exchange rate inquiry on the same basis. Read along the horizontal lines to see where the two cases diverge.

data.notes: There are two criteria for distinguishing between questions that require up-to-dateness and those that do not. Is the answer contained in the question, and does the value change over time? The instructor's conclusion is that receipts are a matter of input format and exchange rates are a matter of knowledge cutoffs. If you first distinguish the nature of the problem like this, you will not be confused about which function to use, and the reason why the results were different for the same AI can be explained at a glance. For questions like exchange rates, don't trust values ​​you get without searching, make sure you have the source.

screens.outro: I will organize the comparisons into one.

screens.title: Criteria for viewing input format and knowledge point together
screens.lead: Let's summarize what has been said so far into two questions.

paragraphs: Before asking AI to do something, ask two things: First, is the necessary information included in the input? You don't need up-to-date information if you can already deliver it to your model in a format the model can receive, such as a photo, file, or voice.

Second, does the answer lie in the world after learning? The model alone cannot know values ​​that change over time, such as today's exchange rate, news announced yesterday, or a policy that was just changed. In this case, you should turn on the web search or hand over the latest materials directly.

The reason it became a receipt and not yesterday's news in the first scene was not a contradiction, but because the answers to these two questions were different. Lastly, knowing that your model can read the input is not the same as saying it read it accurately, so you need to get into the habit of matching important values ​​to the original.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: All the model knows is up to the point of training. Questions that require up-to-date information require a separate connection, such as Search.

glossary.def: This method accepts not only text but also various formats such as images, files, and voices as input.
This is the last point in time at which the model learned information. What happens after this point is not reflected without tools.
It is a tool that finds the latest information from the Internet and attaches it to the model to answer with the source.
A wording from the OpenAI document that refers to the model's ability to analyze images.

misconceptions.myth: Since it can read images, it can read anything accurately.
misconceptions.fact: There is a difference between being able to read and reading accurately. Blurry text or folded areas can be misreading, so check important values ​​against the original.

misconceptions.myth: AI is always connected to the Internet.
misconceptions.fact: Find the latest information only when the search tool is turned on. When you answer without searching, you are only basing your answer on what you learned during the course.

misconceptions.myth: I know exactly what happened before the base date.
misconceptions.fact: Even before the reference date, the model may be incorrect or contain fabricated information. Base dates only indicate the end of a range of knowledge and do not guarantee accuracy.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: In addition to text, the model can receive input in several formats, such as images, files, and audio.
What the model knows is up to the knowledge cutoff, which is the point of learning.
Questions that require up-to-date information require a separate connection, such as a web search.
First determine whether the question requires up-to-dateness, and check the reads against the original.

checks.q: ‘What is the total of this receipt photo?’ and ‘What is today’s exchange rate?’ Which of the following is an appropriate explanation for the two questions?

Receipts are a matter of input format, and exchange rates are a matter of knowledge cutoff.
Both can only be answered if you have a web search connection
Exchange rates can be accurately retrieved from the knowledge learned by the model.
checks.explain: Receipts are solved through multimodal input because the answer is in the photo. Since the exchange rate is a value that changes over time, a connection such as a web search is required to reflect the period after the learning point.

wrong.0: Exchange rates are not resolved through images.
wrong.2: Receipts are resolved only with images and no search is required.
wrong.3: The exchange rate is only the value at the time of learning and is not the current value.
